content: Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) is defined as menstrual blood loss that women perceive as excessive, which can negatively impact their physical, emotional, social, and material quality of life. This condition is considered HMB when it occurs without any underlying systemic or gynecological disease. The first-line treatment for HMB typically involves medical management to avoid unnecessary surgical interventions. Among the various medications available, oral progestogens were historically the most commonly prescribed agents for reducing HMB. This review evaluates the effectiveness of two different types and regimens of oral progestogens in managing ovulatory HMB. It is an update of a Cochrane review originally published in 1998 and last updated in 2007. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness, safety, and tolerability of oral progestogen therapy in reducing menstrual blood loss in women of reproductive age with HMB. The review specifically examined two regimens: short-cycle therapy (administered during the luteal phase) and long-cycle therapy (administered for 21 days per menstrual cycle). A comprehensive search was conducted in January 2019 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and PsycInfo, as well as trial registries and other sources of unpublished or grey literature. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing cyclical oral progestogens with other treatments for HMB were included. Two reviewers independently selected trials, assessed their risk of bias, and extracted data. Adverse events were only analyzed if they were specifically reported in the included trials. The primary outcomes were menstrual blood loss and satisfaction with treatment, while secondary outcomes included the number of bleeding days, quality of life, compliance, acceptability, adverse events, and costs. The review included 15 RCTs involving a total of 1,071 women. Most participants were aware of the treatment they were receiving, which may have influenced their perceptions of menstrual blood loss and satisfaction. The quality of the included trials varied, and no RCTs compared progestogen treatment with placebo. Comparisons between oral progestogens and other medical therapies were analyzed separately based on the regimen used. Short-cycle progestogen therapy, involving medroxyprogesterone acetate or norethisterone administered for 7 to 10 days during the luteal phase (days 15 to 19 of the menstrual cycle), was found to be less effective than other medical therapies, such as tranexamic acid, danazol, and the progestogen-releasing intrauterine system (Pg-IUS, which has been off the market since 2001). These therapies were superior in reducing menstrual blood loss. Women receiving short-cycle progestogen therapy experienced a greater number of bleeding days compared to those on other treatments. Satisfaction and quality of life were similar between groups. Adverse events, such as gastrointestinal symptoms and weight gain, were more common with danazol compared to progestogen therapy. However, danazol is no longer widely used for HMB treatment. Long-cycle progestogen therapy, involving medroxyprogesterone acetate or norethisterone administered from day 5 to day 26 of the menstrual cycle, was also less effective than the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS), tranexamic acid, and ormeloxifene in reducing menstrual blood loss. However, it may have similar effectiveness to the combined vaginal ring. There was no significant difference in the occurrence of headaches between long-cycle progestogen therapy and other medical treatments. Breakthrough bleeding or spotting was more common in women using the LNG-IUS compared to those on progestogen therapy. No trials reported on the number of bleeding days or quality of life for this comparison. The evidence supporting these findings was of low or very low quality, which limits the certainty of the conclusions. The results may change if additional trials are identified in the future. In conclusion, lowor very low-quality evidence suggests that short-cycle progestogen therapy is less effective than other medical treatments, such as tranexamic acid, danazol, and the Pg-IUS, in reducing menstrual blood loss. Similarly, long-cycle progestogen therapy is inferior to the LNG-IUS, tranexamic acid, and ormeloxifene but may be comparable to the combined vaginal ring in terms of reducing menstrual blood loss.
